name: Adam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 27, a team lead wiring homes and repairing small business premises. I've a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I get the difficult faults as well as checking the junior's work. My partner Rosa and I have no children; my pay is typical and we have three months of expenses saved, but the firm's lost two regular shop-refit customers and overtime has already thinned. There are some other electrical firms nearby, though I haven't got an offer; I use AI now and then to draft a materials list after someone has shown me it works, and checking the list is still my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that ordinary repair work still needs doing, so let's finish the jobs customers actually booked. I wouldn't blame every empty afternoon on AI. We've lost shop-refit customers already, and that's a real business problem whether the software is clever or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the order book before your technology story even starts. Three months in the bank helps, but I don't want to spend those savings pretending overtime will return next week. My basic pay covers our essentials at present; another cut in hours would force choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop sending 80 a month to our holiday pot and put it in the emergency account instead. Over the next year I'd keep leading repair jobs and check the firm's booked hours with my manager every month. I'd use the occasional checked materials list as I do now, rather than buy new software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, though not helpless. I can still do work I'm proud of, but the empty lines in next month's diary catch my eye. A quiet AI story doesn't fill our electrical firm's job diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household spending would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I would drop the holiday first, not the rent or the travel that gets us to work. My partner works on the front desk at a sports centre, on fixed hours for now. I wouldn't assume another wage stays safe forever, but it's still coming in today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you ask your manager for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager whether the basic rota is staying whole and how many repairs are actually confirmed. I don't want customer names or private accounts. I need enough notice to change our household spending before the money goes out.

say: I'd tell the team **booked repairs** still matter when the AI story is quiet.
I'd name the lost **shop-refit customers** rather than blaming every empty afternoon on software.
think: I'm already anxious about the **order book**, even though basic pay currently covers essentials.
Three months of savings helps, but I can't assume **overtime returns** before another hours cut.
do: Redirect **80 monthly** from the holiday pot into emergency savings now.
Keep leading **repairs** and check confirmed hours with the manager each month.
feel: **Anxious but capable**, watching empty diary space without losing pride in finished electrical work.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story doesn't fill our electrical firm's job diary.
fieldNote: His **existing order-book worry** sets the baseline; the scenario does not erase current income uncertainty.
He redirects a real **holiday contribution**, so the saving action represents new emergency funds rather than retained cash.

steps.text: Redirect the 80 monthly holiday contribution into emergency savings
Continue leading repairs and checking confirmed hours each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's test the estimating system against the work before trusting the promised saving. We still have to find the damaged cable and make the supply safe. A quicker quote is useful only if the repair can be done properly for the time allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on part protects much of my day for now, but it doesn't protect the price we can charge. With the order book already weak, I could see the firm reducing hours instead of replacing people outright. I'm open to a proven tool, not to being paid less while discovering its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a four-week trial of the AI materials assistant with my manager checking the results alongside me. During the first year I'd record shortages and unused parts on twenty jobs before recommending it for regular use. I'd keep putting the holiday 80 into emergency savings while our wages allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit interested as well. A reliable list could stop the second van trip I hate. I just don't want that improvement used as proof that we can lose a day's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as checking the assistant properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the suggested parts with the actual board and cable route before ordering anything. If a list was wrong, I'd record the correction and who checked it. Twenty clean-looking lists aren't twenty completed jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm points to faster ordering as a reason to cut hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my manager a faster parts order doesn't cancel the testing time. If our hours changed, Rosa and I would revise the budget that week rather than wait for the bank balance to tell us. The emergency saving could shrink if essentials needed the money.

say: I'd test the **estimating system** against completed work before trusting a promised saving.
I'd insist that quicker quotes still leave time for **safe electrical repairs**.
think: Physical work protects much of my day, but a weak order book could still reduce **paid hours**.
I'm willing to test **proven tools**, while refusing to treat unpaid mistakes as progress.
do: Trial the **AI materials assistant** for four weeks with the manager checking results.
Record parts errors on **twenty jobs** during the first year.
Continue the **80 monthly** emergency transfer while wages cover essentials.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, seeing useful fewer trips alongside the risk of reduced pay.
S1.quote: Twenty clean-looking lists aren't twenty completed jobs.
fieldNote: He treats **parts checking** as a real trial rather than adopting automation on appearance alone.
Present **order-book weakness** keeps his own income at risk despite comparatively low thinking-AI exposure.

steps.text: Trial the AI materials assistant and check errors on twenty jobs
Save the holiday 80 monthly while wages cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we need to separate the 2028 office change from robots doing the physical jobs around 2031. I'd want a plan for people whose hours fall between those dates. Saying electricians work with their hands doesn't answer what happens to the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut a large part of my hours once capable robots can handle ordinary installation work. Even before 2031, fewer quotes and office hours could upset how this already shaky business runs. I can make plans, but I don't think three months of savings can cover the gap I picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the 80 transfer going and ask a local technical centre about a building-controls maintenance course, which covers the systems that run heating and lighting. In 2029 I'd enrol only if the course fee was funded and I could keep my basic wage while attending one afternoon a week. I'd also apply for posted maintenance vacancies with actual paid hours, without assuming the course creates one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, because I can see a large loss before I've built a different route. I wake up thinking about the rent rather than the machine. Having a possible course doesn't make the fee or the vacancy real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the course funding never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't spend three months of household cover on tuition. If no fee support or paid release existed, I'd keep working and look for a vacancy that included training on wages. Asking the centre now isn't the same as enrolling now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before taking a maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether any offered maintenance job was mostly software reports or still needed physical checking. Neither is guaranteed safe later, but I should know what I'd be selling my time to do. I'd accept only written hours and pay that cover our essentials.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office work** from later capable robots handling physical installation around 2031.
I'd ask for a **people plan** when hours fall, rather than relying on the hands-on label.
think: I expect **large hour losses** when capable robots handle ordinary installations at an already shaky firm.
Our **three-month cushion** looks too small for the earnings gap I expect.
do: Maintain the **80 transfer** now while asking about building-controls maintenance study.
Enrol in **2029** only with funded fees and basic wages maintained during attendance.
Seek **maintenance vacancies** with written bill-covering hours/pay, or paid-training vacancies if course funding or wage protection is unavailable.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, because possible training doesn't yet supply funding or another wage.
S2.quote: Having a possible course doesn't make the fee or the vacancy real.
fieldNote: The first-year **2029 enrolment** is explicit and conditional; today's enquiry alone is not counted as completed training.
He keeps **funding and wage conditions** attached and does not assume maintenance work is protected from later machines.

steps.text: Keep saving the holiday 80 monthly while essentials remain covered
Enrol in building-controls study in 2029 only with fees and wages funded
Apply for posted maintenance jobs with essential-covering written pay and hours
Seek employer vacancies with paid training if course fee support or wage protection is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to try something while we're still earning. I wouldn't tell the team to abandon repairs tomorrow. Thinking work changes in 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034, so there are two dates to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be less certain of a big personal loss because I could test maintenance work before the later machines arrive. The firm's present shortage of orders still worries me, and my hours could fall well before 2031. I need a plan that survives an ordinary lean winter as well as the big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the 80 monthly transfer now and enrol in the next evening building-controls course only if the fee is covered; evening attendance would let me keep all basic shifts. In 2032 I'd apply for actual maintenance vacancies, checking guaranteed hours and pay against our essentials before accepting. I'd keep the current job until I had a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see smaller decisions instead of one leap. An evening class alongside paid work feels possible. It still doesn't put new customer names into our current repair diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you cannot get the course fee covered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the fee isn't covered, I'd ask which employer vacancies offer paid training and apply for suitable ones. I wouldn't empty the emergency account to make a five-year plan look busy. If neither route exists, I'd keep checking rather than claim I'm retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that preparation fits your current finances?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the confirmed rota for the next month beside the course timetable. If my wage started falling, I'd protect rent first and tell the centre before promising attendance I couldn't finance. Keeping the plan honest matters more than keeping the same date.

say: I'd say **five years** permits testing another route while continuing to earn from repairs.
I'd keep **2031 thinking work** and later capable robots around 2034 distinct.
think: I have more room to avoid a large later loss, but **current orders** still threaten paid hours.
My plan must survive an **ordinary lean winter**, not only the future technology change.
do: Keep saving **80 monthly** now while essentials are covered.
Join the next **evening controls course** only if fees are covered and basic shifts remain intact.
Seek **maintenance vacancies** with written bill-covering hours/pay, or paid-training vacancies if course funding or wage protection is unavailable.
feel: **Anxious with more options**, because evening preparation can fit around a wage that remains uncertain.
S3.quote: I need a plan that survives an ordinary lean winter as well as the big change.
fieldNote: He retains **baseline business risk** even when the longer runway makes later income loss less certain.
Course attendance preserves **fee funding** and all basic shifts; unpaid enquiries never become a claim of retraining.

steps.text: Save 80 monthly while household essentials remain covered
Attend evening controls study only with fees covered and basic shifts intact
Seek maintenance vacancies in 2032 with acceptable written pay and hours
Seek employer vacancies with paid training if course fee support or wage protection is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends the decade is useful, but tomorrow's order book still comes first. I'd prepare a little each year rather than buy every course advertised with a robot on the front. The job has enough real checks without turning forecasts into another full-time duty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I'd still need years of earnings, and robots around 2039 could change any maintenance route too. That later date feels less urgent, but our firm's lost customers haven't come back just because the warning is longer. My own hours could still shrink this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the 80 emergency transfer and enrol in the evening controls course only if fees are covered and all basic shifts stay intact. Each year I'd check actual wages and job advertisements rather than assume more certificates mean more safety. During 2037 I'd apply for suitable posted maintenance work with written pay covering essentials if electrical hours were weakening; I wouldn't resign on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the present business, even though the robot date doesn't sit on my chest. I can talk about 2039 without losing sleep over that date alone. I can't tell the landlord to wait for our contractor to find another customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the monthly saving became unaffordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I would look at the account and confirmed work each month. If bills rose or basic pay fell, we'd reduce the transfer rather than borrow to keep saving. The point is keeping the household going, not winning a savings target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the training remained worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the course tutor and working maintenance staff what tasks changed in the past year. I'd check that against vacancies offering real hours, not just a promotional brochure. If the course stopped fitting actual work, I'd finish the unit already funded and review before spending more.

say: I'd say a **decade's warning** helps, while tomorrow's actual order book still comes first.
I'd avoid buying **every course** simply because its advertising mentions robots.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings, and later robots may affect maintenance work too.
The longer warning doesn't restore **lost customers** or remove the risk of shrinking hours this winter.
do: Continue the **80 transfer** only while basic household bills remain covered.
Enrol in the **evening controls course** only with fees covered and basic shifts intact, reviewing its relevance yearly.
Apply in **2037** for suitable posted maintenance work if hours weaken, requiring acceptable written pay.
feel: **Anxious about present income**, though the later robot date feels less physically overwhelming.
S4.quote: The point is keeping the household going, not winning a savings target.
fieldNote: He preserves **present income uncertainty** rather than allowing the long AI timeline to imply a secure household.
Both **saving and training** stay conditional on real affordability, relevant work and maintained basic shifts.

steps.text: Save 80 monthly only while basic household bills remain covered
Attend funded evening controls study while protecting basic paid shifts
Seek posted maintenance jobs in 2037 if hours weaken, requiring written pay that covers essentials

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the later robot jobs could take a big share of my hours before another route is ready. A training offer with the fee covered and my basic wage maintained would help, and I'd want actual vacancy hours written down. Our emergency account can't be both a college fund and three months of rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how tiring it is to check the work while also checking whether next month's work exists. I like teaching the junior to find a fault properly, and I don't want every conversation with the crew to become a warning. I can care about new tools and still want an ordinary predictable wage.

headlineQuote: Our emergency account can't be both a college fund and three months of rent.
portrait: At **27**, Adam leads electrical work with a technical diploma and master licence, typical pay, and three months of expenses saved.
He and **Rosa**, his partner, have no children; lost refit customers already make his hours uncertain despite some nearby alternatives.
He uses **AI occasionally** after demonstrations and tests a materials assistant against completed jobs rather than trusting polished lists.
Fast change leaves him **alarmed**; longer warnings permit conditional evening study without removing current worries about the firm's order book.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to large later hour losses before a funded route into other paid work is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded training** must preserve basic wages, with actual vacancy hours written down before he changes jobs.
